Online Assessment
The proctored online assessment was conducted on the Hackerrank platform.
Total time alloted was 95 minutes. There were 3 coding questions and each of
them had an individual time limit of 25, 35 & 35 minutes respectively. It was not
permitted to navigate between the questions - we can move to the next
question if we either submit it or the question's time limit gets exhausted.
Sarvagnya Purohit | DE Shaw Interview Experience 2022
1st August, 2022
Similar Strings - 25 minutes time limit
1
If the 2 strings are equal, they are similar
If the 2 strings are unequal and either of them (or both) is of odd length, they
cannot be similar
If the 2 strings are unequal and both of even lengths, then we can split them
to check for similarity if either of the conditions satisfy:
First half of a is similar to second half of b AND second half of a is similar to
first half of b.
First half of a is similar to first half of b AND second half of a is similar to
second half of b.
You've been given 2 strings a and b. You have to determine whether those 2
strings are similar or not. The criteria for similarity of 2 strings was:
1.
2.
3.
a.
b.
Consider the following testcase:
"ab" and "ba" are the 2 strings - since these are of even lengths and they are
unequal, we can observe that the first half of the first string (i.e., "a") and the
second half of the second string (i.e., "a") match. Similarly, the second half of the
first string and first half of the second string match too. Hence, these 2 strings can
be deemed similar.
I solved it using recursion by passing 4 pointers(or rather indexes) - the starting
and ending index of both the strings and checking these conditions recursively.

Subarray Deletion - 35 minutes time limit
2
You've been given an array of positive integers. You're asked to find the number of
subarrays such that removing that subarray results in an array (which must not be
empty) that is sorted in a strictly increasing order.
Consider the following testcase:
Let the array be a = [1, 3, 2] 
If we remove the subarray [2], then we get the resultant array as [1, 3] which is a
sorted array. Similarly, removing the subarray [3] results into the array [1, 2] which
is sorted.
I solved it using sliding window (How? Think of it as how many sorted subarrays
are there - the remaining part of the array can be removed then). The case where
the resulting array must not be empty was also to be considered as an edge case.
Classical 0/1 Knapsack - 35 minutes time limit
3
You've been given 2 arrays of n positive integers - expenditures, cashbacks and
the total money that you have.
Question was the classical 0/1 knapsack question - using the total money that you
have, maximize the cashbacks that you can get by buying the products whose
prices have been given as expenditures. 
You'd to just replace the array names as:
expenditures --> cost
cashbacks --> value
money --> knapsack capacity
Now solve it just like the 0/1 knapsack problem. 
Sarvagnya Purohit | DE Shaw Interview Experience 2022
I was able to solve all the 3 questions and pass all the testcases in them within
the given time limits.
The results of the online assessment were released after 5 days on 6th August,
2022. A total of 17 students were shortlisted for the interviews.

This round was conducted on Hackerrank Codepair. It has several facilities - an
interactive IDE, whiteboard, chat window and voice/video room.
The interviewers asked me to wait for 5-10 minutes initially since a previous
interview was running overtime. Due to this, they did not ask me to introduce
myself and directly jumped into a coding question.
Question 1 (10-15 mins): 
Binary Tree Cameras (LeetCode 968)
You are given the root of a binary tree. We install cameras on the tree nodes
where each camera at a node can monitor its parent, itself, and its immediate
children.
Return the minimum number of cameras needed to monitor all nodes of the tree.
Since there was a whiteboard facility available (you've to request the interviewers
to open it for you), I started explaining the approach (marking the nodes bottom-
up, i.e., while the recursion unwinds, with 3 status flags - either the node has
already been covered by a camera, the node has a camera or the node hasn't
been covered yet) and came up with a recursive formulation in 10-15 minutes.
They seemed satisfied with the explanation and did not ask me to code the
question. Explain your approach and intuition well - don't bother about the
specifics of how you would implement it until they don't ask you.
Question 2 (35-40 minutes):
A system design question (something I'd not even prepared for). I was asked to
design a database pooling utility and make dummy classes in C++ to explain its
functionality.
At the beginning, they asked me if I knew what database pooling was, to which I
answered no (although I'd read a bit about it and had used pgPool in NodeJS, but
since it was a system design question - I'd to understand the requirements
properly and not miss any points or make any unnecessary assumptions). They
formally defined it - "Database connection pooling is a way to reduce the cost of
opening and closing connections by maintaining a “pool” of open connections
that can be passed from database operation to database operation as needed". 
Technical Round 1
8th August, 2022 | 12:30 pm - 1:40 pm
Sarvagnya Purohit | DE Shaw Interview Experience 2022

I was completely blank at this point. No idea how to proceed, none whatsoever.
However, I kept calm and kept thinking out loud. Do not stay silent at any
moment. Sometimes reiterating on the question and your initial thoughts helps
you build your further thought process.
I started with how to establish connections to the Database - made a constructor
in the class with credentials to the database (like username, password, host, port)
as parameters. I initialized them with a constructor initialization list. Then I told
them that I can use the DB Driver/Wire to establish a connection.
Then, I failed miserably at my initial attempts on how do I handle simultaneous
connections. Some of them straightout violated the very definition of what
database pooling was - I did NOT have to establish any connections on the fly. 10-
15 minutes just went understanding this. The interviewers were very friendly and
supportive, providing me with clues and directions whenever I seemed to go off-
track.
After a long while (almost 25 minutes), I came up with the final approach. I would
maintain a specific number of connections while initializing a Pool object (using a
vector of Connection objects). Use a hashset to maintain the indexes of which
connections in the vector were currently free and could be reused. The
requirement was very clear that my class had to be able to respond to multiple
connections running on possibly multiple threads - but by a single user on a
single web application.
Since it took 40 minutes to discuss this question, the interviewers moved on to
the next set of questions although there was a bit more to discuss about how do I
execute queries using the connections I'd established.
Question 3 (15-20 minutes):
A set of questions on DBMS were asked. They started with some SQL Queries
involving the use of a GROUP BY clause, and reusing this query as a subquery in
another JOIN query. 
Then, I was asked about normalization, its need, anomalies it eliminates. I was
asked about the 3 normal forms and given a question on 3NF. I initially took the
wrong candidate key for it (interviewer specified the candidate key as A*B* so I
thought A and B individually were candidate keys but then they clarified AB
together was a candidate key). Always clarify your doubts beforehand and listen
to the question properly. Lastly, a question about indexing was asked and what
data structure is used for it (a B-Tree/B+ Tree). Explain that data structure's
difference from an ordinary Binary Tree.
Think out loud no matter how clueless you are. The interviewers provide you
with enough hints to guide you. Stay comfortable, don't freak out
Sarvagnya Purohit | DE Shaw Interview Experience 2022

I did not expect to get shortlisted for Round 2 but I was eventually shortlisted for
Round 2. The message for that came shortly after I'd my lunch.
Out of the 17 students interviewed for Round 1, 5 students were shortlisted for
Round 2. 
I was firstly greeted by the two interviewers and they were very friendly. Both of
them introduced themselves first and then asked me to introduce myself. Then
they asked me some questions on my resume and the projects/tech-stack I'd
worked on. They asked me about how I plan to prepare for my Smart India
Hackathon Finals project. These initial 7-10 minutes made the environment very
comfortable and friendly.
Question 1 (40 minutes): 
Break Sort (GFG Article) - Read the Problem Statement here.
True to its name, I read the question and it almost broke my hopes of clearing this
round. The question was intimidating at the first glance. The interviewers, however,
guided me extremely well.
I started with a recursive/backtracking approach. I was asked to compute its
time complexity and I got stuck finding its exact complexity since the decision
tree was being pruned haphazaradly. They asked me to move ahead and think of a
better approach. Reading the question gave me a gut feeling that there must be
an adhoc approach to this. I went on with it - traversed the array from left to right
and kept correcting the previous choices based on the current element if it broke
the sorted sequence. Note that 15-20 minutes might already have passed at this
point.
This is where the interviewers dropped 2 crucial hints:
1.
2.
This is where I started dry running on as many testcases as I could on the
whiteboard. I came very close to the optimal approach - start from right of the
array and move left - wherever the sorted sequence breaks, to satisfy that
constraint, use the next element as the upper bound of splitting the current
element
Technical Round 2
8th August, 2022 | 4:00 pm - 5:30 pm
Sarvagnya Purohit | DE Shaw Interview Experience 2022

The max element of that subarray is equal to max_range.
The min element of that subarray is equal to min_range.
The approach I'd come up with was O(N*logN). There were further optimizations
that could be made which the interviewers suggested. They dropped another hint
- "Do I need the minimum moves to sort the array or do I actually need to find the
actual elements?"
Hence, this solution could be eventually optimized to an O(N) time complexity
using some math. It took some time for me to figure out how do I use some
mathematical operations to get (a) the number of moves for splitting the current
element using the next element as upper bound and (b) the smallest element
which I can split into using the current number of moves, so that when I go
leftwards this would be the upper bound I'd have to respect.
Although I took a lot of time, but I was very close to the actual solution. My
explanation wasn't very satisfactory for this question but I made a point to express
my thought process continuously. 
The interviewer is indeed your best friend as you must've read or listened
somewhere. They'd help you and drop crucial hints wherever needed.
Question 2 (20- 25 minutes): 
The question was on sliding window. You're given an array of positive elements
and 2 values - max_range and min_range. You've to find the number of subarrays in
the given array which satisfy the following 2 properties:
1.
2.
The question was a classic sliding window + monotonic queue question.
However, after my experience in the previous question, I went very slow on the
whiteboard and did not want to make any mistakes. I came up with an O(N)
solution in approximately 10 minutes. 
The interviewer then asked me to code this approach. I started coding it using 2
deques (storing indexes rather than elements themselves) during which they
asked me a bit about C++ STL Deques. I'd almost completed the code but since
20 minutes had already passed and I'd implemented all the conditions properly,
they asked me to move on.
Question 3 (10 minutes): 
In these last 10 minutes, they asked me about a set of questions based on
Operating Systems. This was the third time I'd requested them to open a new
whiteboard tab and they happily opened it while having a laugh. They asked me
questions on - demand paging and its need in virtual memory, binary semaphores
and how they work (always use examples in such questions on the whiteboard to
explain the concept better), pipes and message-passing. 
Sarvagnya Purohit | DE Shaw Interview Experience 2022

At the end, they asked if I had any questions for them. I asked them how was the
entire transition to remote work during the COVID-19 lockdown implemented since
it was very fascinating how smoothly huge companies adapted this transition.
They answered in a very friendly manner and talked even about their personal
experiences in the WFH conditions. Ask any questions you might have in the end.
Stress on the word "any" - this is your chance to open up with the interviewer.
The results for this final round came at about 9:40 pm and 2 students were
selected. I was fortunate to be one of them 🙏
Sarvagnya Purohit | DE Shaw Interview Experience 2022
Tips
Stay Calm and Confident. Confidence is given huge weightage in interviews.
Stay hydrated and don't remain hungry during the interview day
Keep speaking your mind - explain your thought process. Don't take any    
 long silent breaks.
Trust yourself and your preparation. Even if you encounter a seemingly
difficult question, the interviewers are kind enough to provide crucial hints.
Interviewers are indeed your friends. Don't get intimidated if you cannot think
about an approach to a question
Related to DSA:
Look for patterns in questions. I had personally used LeetCode Study Plans
(Algorithm I, Algorithm II, DP II, Graph II and Binary Search II - this one is arguably
the best). These mostly cover all patterns. Blind 75 (and an extended
NeetCode's Blind 150) is another resource I'd heavily relied on. Using these, I
was able to identify patterns being used in questions.
Another point I'd want to make is religiously do the Daily LeetCode Challenges.
I'd done these for 2 months and at the end, my very first interview question
(Binary Tree Cameras) was a June LeetCode Daily Challenge which I'd already
solved.
Related to Core CS(OS, DBMS, OOPS):
For both CS/non-CS students - Gate Smashers OS and DBMS is more than
sufficient for both academics and interviews. Don't just binge watch the
lectures but make some notes on OneNote/Notion/Docs (not traditional notes
but screenshots would do - screenshots helped me a lot during revision).
For OOPS, use any resource available online in your language of choice (prefer
C++, Java or Python) and cover the major concepts in it.
